analysis.investment_thesis: DIACABS is a NCLT-resurrection story riding India's power infra boom, with revenue recovering from ₹0 (FY22) to ₹1,115 Cr (FY25) — but at ₹7,884 Cr market cap and P/E of 75x on just ₹34 Cr profit with a technically insolvent balance sheet (equity: -₹714 Cr), the market has priced in perfection for a company that nearly went to zero. This fails every SMILE filter: too large, too expensive, and deeply scarred fundamentals.
key_strengths: Dramatic revenue recovery: ₹0 (FY22) → ₹343 Cr (FY24) → ₹1,115 Cr (FY25), riding India's massive power transmission investment cycle
Promoter holding at 84.02% — extraordinarily high, signals conviction in the restructuring story
Operating cash flow turned positive at ₹77 Cr in FY25, with capex ramping (₹68 Cr) suggesting real capacity expansion
key_risks: Negative equity of -₹714 Cr and negative reserves of -₹767 Cr — the company is technically insolvent; all prior equity was wiped out by ₹805 Cr loss in FY17 alone
Valuation is absurd: P/E 75x, EV/EBITDA 68x on a company with just ₹34 Cr net profit — market cap is 232x FY25 earnings and 7x FY25 revenue
History of catastrophic collapse: revenue fell from ₹3,153 Cr (FY14) to zero, suggesting structural/management failures that aren't priced into the recovery narrative
red_flags: Market cap ₹7,884 Cr — nearly 8x outside Kedia's 1,000 Cr sweet spot; this is not a discoverable small-cap
Negative book value (P/B: -10.95x) — accumulated losses have wiped equity; P/B is meaningless and dangerous here
P/E of 74.9x vs Kedia target of 8-15x — paying growth-stock prices for a distressed-company recovery with zero margin of safety
Borrowings jumped from ₹456 Cr (FY24) to ₹610 Cr (FY25) even as the company just turned profitable — leverage risk on a fragile balance sheet
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Diamond Power Infrastructure is a resurrection story, not a SMILE story. The company essentially went through insolvency proceedings — revenue collapsed from ₹3,153 Cr (FY14) to literally zero (FY22), destroying ₹1,800+ Cr of equity along the way. The recent recovery is real and impressive: ₹1,115 Cr revenue and ₹34 Cr net profit in FY25, EBITDA margins at 12.9%, and positive OCF at ₹77 Cr. India's power transmission buildout (renewables, grid expansion) gives it a genuine tailwind. But paying ₹7,884 Cr for ₹34 Cr of profit — on a company with -₹714 Cr equity — is speculation, not investing.

Every SMILE parameter is violated. Market cap is 8x the upper bound. P/E at 75x is 5x what Kedia would accept even for quality compounders. The negative equity means the business has zero intrinsic book value — any hiccup in execution reverts to crisis. Borrowings are growing (₹610 Cr in FY25 vs ₹456 Cr in FY24) even as the balance sheet remains technically insolvent. The promoter's 84% stake is the only genuine SMILE element, but high promoter holding in a restructured company often reflects diluted equity post-resolution, not conviction buying at current prices. At 1/10th the market cap and 1/5th the P/E, this story might be worth watching — not today.
